mainKeyword: best generator for class a motorhome
guideTitle: Best Generators for Class A Motorhomes (2026)
metaTitle: Best Generators for Class A Motorhomes (2026)
metaDescription: Five portable generators sized for a Class A motorhome backup or supplement: running watts per fuel, outlets, noise and upkeep compared for big coaches.
expertTake: The Westinghouse 9500 is our top pick for a Class A coach because it combines high running watts with a 6.6 gallon tank and a transfer-style 120/240 volt outlet. The WEN 6800 is the value pick if you accept less output for an inverter's quiet. If your coach has a healthy onboard generator, you may only need a smaller portable as a spare.
introParagraphs: A large motorhome rarely relies on a portable generator for daily life, because most carry a built-in unit. The portable machine is the backup when the onboard set is down, or a way to supplement it at a site where you want to avoid running a large engine all night.

That role shapes the shopping. You need enough running watts to handle several air conditioners and a galley, an outlet that matches a heavy-duty inlet, and a machine you can lift out of a basement bay. The right choice depends on how much of the coach you want to power.

products.name: Westinghouse 9500 Peak Watt Dual Fuel Generator, 6.6 Gallon Tank
products.description:
This is the first machine in the lineup that can run most of a Class A coach by itself. With 7,500 rated watts on gasoline and 6,750 on propane, it has enough for two air conditioners and a galley load, and the propane loss is only about 10 percent. The 6.6 gallon tank gives it the longest stretch between refuels of the generators under 9,000 watts.

It provides an L14-30R 120/240 volt outlet, which is a 30 amp connection. That is not the 50 amp plug a large coach uses, so you will need an adapter or a transfer arrangement, and it limits how much of the load the coach can draw through a single cord. It ships with a key fob and a 12 volt battery charger, a useful touch for a machine that will sit.

This is a heavy open-frame unit and needs a wheel kit and a ramp. The battery charger keeps the starter battery alive over winter, and the 6.6 gallon tank needs stabilizer if the unit sits unused. Run it monthly under load and check the oil level before each start. Because a Class A coach has a long shore cord run, use a heavy gauge adapter cord and keep it short, since voltage drop under air conditioner load makes compressors run hot and hard.
products.bestFor: Large coaches that want to run two air conditioners from a portable backup.
pros: 7,500 rated watts runs two air conditioners
Only about 10 percent output loss on propane
Remote start fob and battery charger included
6.6 gallon tank for long unattended runs
cons: Outlet is a 30 amp L14-30R, not a 50 amp plug
Heavy and loud like all open-frame units

products.name: Westinghouse 12500 Watt Dual Fuel Generator, 457cc, Transfer Ready
products.description:
For a Class A coach where three air conditioners and a residential refrigerator can all be running at once, 9,500 rated watts is the ceiling. This unit lists 9,500 on gasoline and 8,500 on propane. The 457cc engine uses a cast iron sleeve, which holds up to long heat-soaked afternoons better than an aluminum bore.

The cost is bulk. It is a large steel frame that two people will struggle to load into a basement bay, so most owners keep it on a trailer hitch carrier or in a garage. Compared with the 9500 model, it adds 2,000 rated watts and a larger engine, but uses the same L14-30R style outlet arrangement plus an RV outlet.

Because a generator this large often serves as home backup too, think about the storage season. Drain the carburetor, charge the starter battery and protect the machine from rain. Parts for the Westinghouse family are widely available, which is a major advantage on the road. If a diesel pusher is your daily home, this is also the unit that can keep a residential refrigerator and the house batteries charging while the onboard set is serviced, and its cast iron sleeve is the reason it tolerates the long idle summers.
products.bestFor: Coaches with three air conditioners that also want home backup.
pros: 9,500 rated watts is the highest sustained output here
Cast iron sleeve suits long hot runs
Propane drops only to 8,500 rated watts
Widely available parts and service
cons: Too heavy for a basement bay

products.name: AIVOLT 8000W Dual Fuel Inverter Generator, 120/240V, 62 dBA
products.description:
A 322cc inverter that claims 8,000 watts and 62 dBA at 23 feet is an unusual combination, and it is the reason this machine suits a Class A owner who parks in resorts. A diesel pusher's onboard generator makes noise you cannot change, while this portable unit lets you run quietly at night.

The automatic fuel switching moves between propane and gasoline, so a bottle running empty does not shut down the coach. It is labeled 50 amp RV ready with 120/240 volt output, which fits a big coach inlet more naturally than the 30 amp outlets on the Westinghouse units.

The trade is that an inverter of this size carries a lot of electronics, and the brand has a short service record. Keep it out of the rain, maintain airflow around the vents, and check what the warranty covers. At 8,000 watts it will not run three air conditioners together, so manage loads. On paper it gives up about 500 rated watts to the Westinghouse 9500, yet it runs far quieter, and for a coach that sits at a resort for a week that quiet is often worth more than the watts.
products.bestFor: Class A owners who want a quiet 50 amp class machine.
pros: 62 dBA at 23 feet is quiet for 8,000 watts
120/240 volt output with 50 amp RV readiness
Automatic propane to gasoline switching
Clean inverter power for electronics
cons: Brand has a short service record
Cannot run three air conditioners together

products.name: WEN 6800 Watt Dual Fuel RV Ready Inverter, CO Watchdog
products.description:
At 5,100 rated watts on gasoline and 4,500 on propane, the WEN can run one or two air conditioners in a Class A coach as a supplement rather than a full replacement. Its strength is the inverter design and the safety systems: the Watchdog sensor shuts the engine off if carbon monoxide builds up near the machine.

The bonded-neutral 240 volt configuration is designed for low-power Level 2 vehicle charging, which a Class A owner towing a plug-in car behind the coach might use. That is a niche feature, but it shows the engineering priority is flexibility.

It is lighter than the Westinghouse models and easier to carry in a bay, but you give up more than 4,000 watts of output compared with the 9500 model. Expect to manage loads carefully and run the other air conditioner only when the first is stable. A soft start kit on each roof unit is a cheap upgrade that cuts the starting surge, and with it this machine can handle two units where it otherwise would trip on a simultaneous start.
products.bestFor: Coaches that need a quieter, supplemental generator for part of the load.
pros: CO Watchdog shutoff improves safety
5,100 rated watts handles one or two air conditioners
Inverter keeps noise modest
Lighter than the open-frame giants
cons: Cannot match the 9,500 watt units on output

products.name: WEN DF450i 4500 Watt Dual Fuel RV Ready Inverter, 212cc
products.description:
This is the smallest machine in the guide and its role is specific: a lightweight, quiet backup that can keep the coach's fridge, lights and one air conditioner alive if the onboard generator fails. At 3,500 rated watts on gasoline and 3,150 on propane it will not run the whole coach.

Automatic fuel selection moves from propane to gasoline, and the 58 dBA rating at quarter load and 22 feet is quiet. The EPA III and CARB compliant 212cc engine means it can be used in states with strict rules, which matters if you cross California.

It weighs far less than the 9500 model, so one person can load it. Treat it as insurance for a coach, and keep it ready with fresh fuel and a charged start system. Compared with the 56450iX gas-only cousin, the dual fuel version gives you propane for storage. Keep a small propane cylinder with it in the bay, and exercise it quarterly so you know it starts when the onboard set does not.
products.bestFor: Class A owners who want a light spare in case the onboard set fails.

58 dBA at quarter load and 22 feet
EPA III and CARB compliant engine
Light enough for one person to lift

buyingCriteria.explanation: Most Class A coaches carry a built-in generator, so a portable acts as a backup or a supplement. A backup only needs to run essentials, like the 3,500 watt WEN DF450i. A supplement that shares the load with the onboard unit wants 5,000 watts or more, like the WEN 6800 at 5,100 rated.

A typical Class A has two or three 13,500 to 15,000 BTU roof units. Each draws about 1,500 watts running and 2,500 to 3,000 at start. Three units together demand the 9,500 rated watts of the Westinghouse 12500, while two fit the 7,500 rated Westinghouse 9500.

A big coach inlet is a 50 amp plug, but many portable units offer only a 30 amp L14-30R. The Westinghouse 9500 and 12500 give an L14-30R, while the AIVOLT 8000 is labeled 50 amp RV ready. An adapter does not raise the capacity; it only matches the plug, so check the circuit rating.

A 6.6 gallon tank on the 9500 or a 9.5 gallon tank on larger units reduces refueling trips. Propane lowers output by 10 to 12 percent, such as 7,500 down to 6,750 rated watts on the 9500. Size on the propane figure if you rely on it.

A 12,500 watt open frame can weigh well over 200 pounds, which excludes a basement bay and needs a hitch carrier or a ramp. The WEN DF450i is far lighter and fits a bay. Weigh how often you will actually deploy it before choosing size, and remember that a machine too heavy to move safely tends to stay in the garage when you need it. A rolling ramp and a second person solve most of that.

Class A coaches often stay at resorts with strict quiet hours. The AIVOLT 8000 lists 62 dBA at 23 feet and the DF450i 58 dBA at quarter load. Open-frame units like the Westinghouse 12500 are far louder and may be banned at some sites.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to a big coach
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rated watts to the demand of two or three air conditioners plus a galley. The Westinghouse 12500 at 9,500 rated watts was the only one that comfortably covers three. Smaller units were treated as supplements.

howWeEvaluated.title: Inlet compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked the outlet types against a 50 amp RV inlet. The AIVOLT 8000 is labeled 50 amp ready while the Westinghouse models use a 30 amp locking outlet and need an adapter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel behaviour
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tank sizes, propane output and fuel switching. The 6.6 gallon tank on the Westinghouse 9500 and the automatic switching on the WEN DF450i were highlighted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Stated weights and frame types were used to judge storage. Open frames over 200 pounds need a carrier or ramp. The DF450i fits a basement bay.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and rules
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored published noise figures with a distance and load, including 62 dBA at 23 feet for the AIVOLT and 58 dBA at 22 feet for the WEN DF450i. Resort rules were part of the weighting, because a coach that cannot run its generator at the site gains nothing from extra watts.

A 6.6 gallon tank sitting for months gums the carburetor. Use stabilizer or run it dry.
Cracked lines leak fuel and waste propane. Replace any hardened hose.

faq.q: Does a Class A motorhome need a portable generator?
faq.a: Not if the onboard generator is healthy. A portable is a backup if that unit fails, or a supplement when you want to avoid running a large engine overnight.

faq.q: How many watts do I need for a Class A?
faq.a: Two air conditioners and a galley need about 6,000 to 7,500 watts, while three need around 9,500. Check the nameplates on your units and add the starting surge.

faq.q: Which is the best budget pick?
faq.a: The WEN DF450i is the lowest cost here and works as a spare. The WEN 6800 offers more output at a mid price.

faq.q: Can a 30 amp outlet run a 50 amp coach?
faq.a: With an adapter it can feed the coach, but only up to 3,600 watts. It will not run multiple air conditioners.

faq.q: Is propane enough for a Class A?
faq.a: On the Westinghouse 9500 propane gives 6,750 rated watts, enough for two air conditioners. Larger demands need gasoline.

faq.q: Where do I store a large generator?
faq.a: Many owners use a hitch carrier or keep it in a garage. Lighter units like the WEN DF450i fit a basement bay. Never run any generator in an enclosed bay.
